The main intended benefit is to show which immunosuppressed people have not developed antibodies, so policy makers and clinicians can consider extra protection for them.

DARS-NIC-620484-W0B2K.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised patient-level hospital, emergency care, diagnostic imaging and death registration records for people enrolled in the EVAREST study. It allows following their heart-related care and outcomes after a stress echocardiogram (a heart test) to assess how accurate the test is and how it is used across the UK. The aim is to find areas for improvement and so reduce unnecessary further procedures. Two manuscripts using the data have already been published.

DARS-NIC-622485-S4F5C.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers the use of NHS hospital, emergency care and death registration records for a clinical trial of a cerebral embolic protection device used during transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). It allows the trial to look at long-term outcomes for trial participants, which groups face a higher risk of stroke, and whether using the device is cost-effective for the NHS. The data is for helping patients make evidence-informed decisions about their care.

DARS-NIC-623799-T2J4F.summary: ModernaTX, Inc's agreement covers the use of details people gave through the NHS "Sign Up to be Contacted about Coronavirus Vaccine Studies" service, including age, sex, location, employment and health answers. The main intended benefit is faster recruitment, helping to speed up delivery of an effective vaccine.

DARS-NIC-62448-Z8K5T.summary: The University of Sheffield's agreement covers hospital records for accident and emergency, admitted patient care and critical care (Hospital Episode Statistics). DARS-NIC-625841-T2V6N.summary: Cancer Research UK, with the University of Leeds added as a data processor, is permitted to use non-identifiable national radiotherapy data collected during the COVID-19 pandemic. The aim is to give evidence to help health services recover and prepare for future pandemics.

DARS-NIC-626153-S6J6V.summary: King's College London's agreement covers cancer registration data from the National Disease Registration Service (NDRS) for YORKSURe, a feasibility trial of urine self-testing for blood in the urine to detect bladder cancer earlier in people at high risk of dying from it in Yorkshire. The findings are intended to show whether a larger trial is viable, which could lead to earlier detection and better survival.

The aim is to understand patterns of health need and develop better care. The linked data allow the Trust to identify likely palliative care needs in the last year of life and assess inequalities in access to palliative care services.

DARS-NIC-627125-B9N0Z.summary: NHS South Yorkshire ICB, a sub-ICB location, has an agreement covering pseudonymised hospital, community, mental health, maternity, prescribing, social care and death and birth registration data for the South Yorkshire and Bassetlaw area. DARS-NIC-628591-K2Q2V.summary: The University of Bristol's agreement covers identifiable hospital records (admitted patient care, outpatients and emergency care) for about 600 people with Parkinson's disease who joined the CHIEF-PD trial. The records show which hospital stays were caused by falls and what hospital care cost over 12 months. The data is for testing whether rivastigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, prevents falls compared with a placebo and is cost-effective for the NHS. The findings are intended to inform NICE guidance on Parkinson's care.

DARS-NIC-628636-Y3B1N.summary: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust and the University of Cambridge's agreement covers identifiable but not directly identifying NHS England cancer data, covering registrations, treatments, scans, waiting times, radiotherapy and patient experience. The data is for studying survival among people treated for breast cancer at Addenbrooke's Hospital over ten years. The aim is to compare the service with national figures and understand differences by treatment and demographic factors. This is expected to support recommendations to improve breast cancer care.

DARS-NIC-629056-F4L4B.summary: The University of Warwick's agreement covers the use of demographic data from NHS Digital to identify and invite adults who were in hospital with COVID-19 and still have symptoms after three months (long Covid) to join the REGAIN trial. The trial tests whether an eight-week online exercise and mental health support programme helps, compared with a single online advice session. The main intended benefit is faster recruitment, so results can guide long Covid rehabilitation while still relevant.

DARS-NIC-630656-V9W9M.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers NHS Business Services Authority records of medicines dispensed in primary care, plus basic demographic details (vital status, current address and GP surgery), for ORION-4, a trial of the cholesterol-lowering drug inclisiran. The data is for checking how well routine medicines data matches trial records and supporting contact with participants. The main intended benefit is showing whether inclisiran is safe and effective for people with cardiovascular disease.

DARS-NIC-631605-F2H3M.summary: The Office for National Statistics (ONS) agreement covers the use of maternity records from the Maternity Services Data Set to produce official statistics. The data is for research on COVID-19 and pregnancy, child and maternal health, and the future of population and census statistics. The main intended benefit is better evidence for government policy and public health decisions. Research has produced admin-based ethnicity statistics for England and Wales.

DARS-NIC-63161-C6S8V.summary: NHS Rotherham CCG's agreement covers hospital activity data from the Secondary Uses Service (SUS), covering accident and emergency, inpatient and outpatient care, together with primary care data. The main intended benefit is better planning and fewer avoidable emergency admissions.

The data is for giving policymakers and clinicians evidence to help improve care and support for children and young people.

The main stated benefit is avoiding distress.

DARS-NIC-63347-R8J2M.summary: The Royal College of Anaesthetists's agreement covers identifiable hospital admission, critical care and death registration records for adults in the PQIP study who have had major planned non-cardiac surgery. The agreement allows the records to be linked to study data to measure complications, recovery and survival after surgery, and to give hospitals feedback on care quality. The aim is fewer complications and better outcomes. Reported benefits include an enhanced recovery approach that NHS England adopted as a CQUIN financial target for Trusts.

DARS-NIC-633657-S7Z5R.summary: The Office for National Statistics (ONS)'s agreement covers use of the Community Services Data Set, which holds information on community health services. The agreement allows the data to be used for research into whether population statistics, including on health and ethnicity, can be produced from administrative data. This research will form part of the evidence for the 2023 National Statistician's Recommendation on whether to hold another traditional Census in 2031.

DARS-NIC-634901-B4H8K.summary: Barts Health NHS Trust's agreement covers identifiable hospital admission records (Hospital Episode Statistics Admitted Patient Care) and civil registration death records for people in England with Marfan syndrome. The main intended benefit is better understanding of their care needs, to help guide services and treatment.

The main intended benefit is faster recruitment, helping speed up the delivery of an effective vaccine.

The main intended benefit is evidence to guide treatment and policy for pneumonia patients.

DARS-NIC-63798-B9T0B.summary: City of Westminster's agreement covers the use of hospital and emergency care records (Hospital Episode Statistics and the Emergency Care Data Set) for its public health work. The agreement allows the data to produce needs assessments, health strategies, public health advice to NHS commissioners and the Director of Public Health's annual report. The data is for locally focused analysis of health and health inequalities. Annual public health reports have been published, and mortality data has helped shape local action on health inequalities.

DARS-NIC-63997-N3N7R.summary: London Borough of Bexley's agreement covers civil registration data on births and deaths, plus primary care mortality data, which includes identifiable details. The agreement allows the data to be used to understand local health needs, plan services and protect public health, including through suicide audits. The aim is to tailor services and reduce health inequalities and premature deaths. The council used the mortality data in its Suicide Audit to understand risk characteristics and better target suicide prevention.

DARS-NIC-641622-S4C1Q.summary: The University of Newcastle upon Tyne's agreement covers NHS hospital, emergency care, community, mental health and psychological therapy records, plus death registration data. It allows the study of how COVID-19 and lockdowns changed the use of mental health services by people in the most deprived communities in North East and North Cumbria, and how this relates to their health outcomes. The data is for helping policy-makers and service planners meet the needs of underserved groups.

DARS-NIC-642373-Z3P7N.summary: Imperial College London's agreement covers pseudonymised maternity records from the Maternity Services Data Set, covering 2015 to 2023. The data is for studying which factors in maternity care contribute to differences in pregnancy outcomes, including deaths, between ethnic groups, and for assessing the quality and completeness of the data. The main intended benefit is evidence to help improve maternity services and reduce excess mortality among women and babies.

DARS-NIC-643421-J9T3M.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers the use of identifiable cancer registration, death registration and demographic data on about 1,400 male doctors in the British Doctors Study. The data is for following them up to examine how smoking, stopping smoking and daily aspirin affect cancer, other diseases and cause of death. The aim is to add evidence on preventing diseases such as cancer and cardiovascular disease. Earlier results from the study are reported to have influenced national and personal decisions about quitting smoking.

DARS-NIC-64474-V4B2D.summary: St George's Hospital Medical School's agreement covers linked, de-identified hospital admission, critical care, death registration and demographic records for children born with a congenital anomaly, drawn from five regional registers in England. The data is for building a research database to study these children's long-term survival, health and educational outcomes. The main intended benefit is helping parents understand their children's needs, prospects and life chances.

DARS-NIC-644891-N5T3S.summary: University College London's agreement covers identifiable NHS England data on deaths, cancer registrations and medicines dispensed in primary care. The data covers people who took part in the AspECT trial and are included in this follow-up study. The agreement allows the data to be used to follow their long-term outcomes, including oesophageal cancer and death, and to see how aspirin and proton pump inhibitor use affected them. The main intended benefit is stronger evidence on preventing oesophageal cancer in people with Barrett's oesophagus.

DARS-NIC-64572-X0Q4D.summary: The National Institute for Cardiovascular Outcomes Research's agreement covers the use of tabulated hospital-level Hospital Episode Statistics Admitted Patient Care data, which are counts of patients and not patient-level records. The agreement allows the data to be used to check how many heart attack patients each hospital submits to the national heart attack audit (MINAP) compared with those coded in hospital records. The main intended benefit is better audit data quality and fairer comparisons between hospitals. Case ascertainment rates have been published annually since 2017, revealing wide variation between hospitals.

DARS-NIC-647363-F3R4R.summary: The University of Oxford's Oxford Vaccine Group's agreement covers NHS England's recruitment service, which supplies a mailing list of people matched by age and postcode area, to invite about 4,000 potential volunteers to a malaria vaccine trial. The trial is for testing the safety and effectiveness of a candidate vaccine, including with volunteers deliberately infected under controlled conditions. The data is for identifying and inviting participants only, to help reach the recruitment target. The trial may contribute to a safe, effective malaria vaccine.

DARS-NIC-648118-L0Q2Z.summary: King's College London's agreement covers hospital, emergency care and COVID-19 vaccination status records, linked to a South London register of mothers and children called eLIXIR. The agreement allows the data to be used for approved research on maternal, child and mental health, including pregnancy complications, long-term health and vaccine uptake among pregnant women. The aim is evidence to inform clinical guidelines, health services and public health policy.

DARS-NIC-648561-Z8L8M.summary: Archus Limited, a consultancy advising the NHS, has an agreement covering patient-level hospital data on emergency care, admitted patients, critical care and outpatients. The agreement allows the data to be used to model future healthcare needs by place and population, supporting service redesign and the planning of hospital facilities. The main intended benefit is better capacity planning and more informed decisions on healthcare buildings and services. So far, the data has been used in a national analysis of robotic assisted surgery, highlighting potential savings and patient outcome improvements.

DARS-NIC-649110-Z5S0L.summary: The University of Birmingham's agreement covers pseudonymised hospital records (admissions, accident and emergency, critical care and outpatient data) for people who took part in the CReST2 trial. The trial compares covered and uncovered stents for bowel obstruction caused by colorectal cancer in patients not fit for major surgery. The data is for estimating NHS costs for each stent type. The aim is to show which stent offers better value for money and quality of life.

DARS-NIC-650245-T6C6T.summary: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust's agreement covers identifiable hospital admission records and demographic data, including date of death, for 183 adults who survived intensive care with sepsis and took part in a clinical trial. The data is for checking who was readmitted to hospital with an infection, estimating hospital costs and measuring survival. It will show whether a single pneumococcal vaccine reduces infections and rehospitalisation after sepsis, and whether a larger future trial is worthwhile.

DARS-NIC-650291-P6N5H.summary: The University of Surrey's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised data from the Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Survey (APMS), combining the 2007 and 2014 surveys. The research examines how sleep problems, self-harm and suicide are linked, and whether difficulty managing emotions (emotion dysregulation) plays a part. The main intended benefit is a clearer understanding that could support better-targeted care for adults with poor sleep and emotion dysregulation.

DARS-NIC-651348-Z0N4H.summary: Swansea University's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised hospital, emergency care, critical care and death registration records for about 550,000 patients who used participating ambulance services. The agreement allows comparison of ethnic minority and White British people with injuries, looking at the care they receive and their outcomes over six months, and at how complete ethnicity records are. The intended benefit is evidence to help policy makers and care providers improve injury care for ethnic minority populations.

DARS-NIC-651660-J5T6C.summary: Grail Bio UK Ltd, a commercial company working with Queen Mary University of London, is permitted to use demographic data (vital status and current addresses) for people taking part in the NHS-Galleri cancer screening trial. The agreement allows this data to update the participant list, remove people who have died and send a thank-you letter and follow-up appointment invitations. The data is for keeping participants informed and helping them stay in the trial.

DARS-NIC-651858-F5H2J.summary: King's College London's agreement covers pseudonymised maternity records for mothers and babies, along with civil registrations of death, for 2017/18 to 2022/23. The data is for understanding how maternity outcomes, such as eclampsia, caesarean section and baby deaths, vary by ethnic group, NHS trust and region. The intended main benefit is evidence to help policymakers and clinicians tailor maternity care and reduce unfair differences in outcomes.

DARS-NIC-653950-W8D4Z.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers identifiable NHS England data, including hospital, death, cancer registration and demographic records, for 1,441 consenting participants in the Oxford Vascular Study. The study follows people in eight Oxfordshire GP practices after stroke, TIA, acute coronary syndrome and other vascular events, to measure outcomes and costs of care. The data is for improving prevention, diagnosis and treatment. Study findings have already informed national stroke guidelines.

DARS-NIC-654590-Y0S1H.summary: Cardiff University's agreement covers pseudonymised hospital admission records and death registration data for about 3,000 patients who took liothyronine (T3) or similar thyroid treatments. The study examines whether long-term T3 use for underactive thyroid affects survival or raises the risk of heart attacks, heart rhythm problems, heart failure or strokes, compared with patients on levothyroxine (T4). If T3 is shown to be safe, it could widen treatment options for patients who do not feel better on T4 and inform future guidelines.

DARS-NIC-655024-S2H5Q.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers the use of NHS England contact and demographic details, plus aggregate data quality reports, to identify and invite people with type 2 diabetes to join the ASCEND PLUS clinical trial. The trial tests whether the drug oral semaglutide reduces heart attacks, strokes and other diabetes complications, which could change treatment guidelines. Recruitment has reportedly been two to three times faster than the original ASCEND trial, with 9,200 people randomised by November 2024.

DARS-NIC-655446-P9K9Q.summary: Adelphi Group Limited, a consultancy working for Merck Sharp & Dohme (MSD) Medical Affairs UK, has an agreement covering pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, imaging, radiotherapy and chemotherapy data on adults diagnosed with stage II melanoma between 2015 and early 2018. The agreement allows study of patients' characteristics, the treatments they receive and the cost of their care to the NHS. The data is for filling a gap in evidence on the stage II melanoma patient pathway, to support decisions on care and treatment.

DARS-NIC-656749-G8K4G.summary: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust's agreement covers pseudonymised cancer registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for about 85,000 people who had a solid organ transplant. The agreement allows linking these with other existing records to study cancer after transplantation, including cancer types, deaths and hospital care. The main intended benefit is evidence to inform care guidelines and help counsel people before a transplant.

DARS-NIC-656750-K1X5M.summary: Imperial College London's Cancer Screening and Prevention Research Group's agreement covers the use of NDRS cancer registration data, linked to bowel screening records for consenting participants. The data is for testing whether yearly faecal immunochemical tests (FIT) can safely replace three-yearly colonoscopies for people with intermediate adenomas, and for examining acceptability and costs. The aim is to inform surveillance guidelines. The study's results have been published, including in the journal Gut in 2019, and report that annual FIT could cut colonoscopies by 71% and reduce NHS costs.

DARS-NIC-656751-H5K0Y.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised NHS England cancer registration, cancer pathway, treatment and linked hospital records for more than 100,000 women who have consented to take part in the Generations Study. The data is for studying genetic and environmental risk factors for cancer, mainly breast cancer, and outcomes after diagnosis. The aim is to add evidence that could shape guidance on prevention and care. Published papers have already appeared, including a large pooled analysis of physical activity and premenopausal breast cancer.

DARS-NIC-656752-G2L2P.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers identifiable National Disease Registration Service cancer registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for about 4.5 million women in the AgeX Trial. The trial tests the risks and benefits of extra NHS breast screening invitations at ages 47-49 and 71-73. The findings are intended to help the UK government decide whether to widen the age range for routine breast screening.

DARS-NIC-656754-C6S5Q.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers NHS England cancer registration data, linked to its EPIC-Oxford cohort of 60,642 adults, to study how diet, especially vegetarian and vegan diets, affects long-term health. The data is for giving reliable evidence to inform public and NHS dietary advice. Findings have been published in journals such as the BMJ and used in evidence reviewed by the Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition.

DARS-NIC-656755-W4N5C.summary: Queen Mary University of London, an academic institution, has an agreement covering identifiable National Disease Registration Service cancer registration data on people diagnosed with colorectal cancer in 2012 and 2013. The data is for a case-control study evaluating the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme, and the agreement allows further analyses on other disease stages and checks for possible biases. The main intended benefit is to estimate the programme's effect on late-stage disease. The team published results in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute (2022) showing a reduction in Dukes D stage cancer with screening.

DARS-NIC-656757-J8V9D.summary: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine's agreement covers pseudonymised data on cancer registrations, hospital care, diagnostic imaging, treatments and patient surveys. The data is for studying why inequalities in cancer care and survival arise and persist in England, including the roles of patient, tumour, clinical and healthcare system factors. The aim is to inform strategies that reduce these inequalities. Earlier findings reported by the team showed that differences by deprivation, age or gender were only partly explained by patient factors, which points to barriers within the healthcare system.

DARS-NIC-656758-N4H9Y.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised national cancer registration, treatment, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and hospital data on women in England diagnosed with breast cancer. The data is for studying how four breast cancer subtypes vary by age, ethnicity and other characteristics, and how treatment and survival differ. The aim is to identify gaps in care and support tailored treatment. Three peer-reviewed papers have been published, and results have been presented at conferences.

DARS-NIC-656760-F8Y3C.summary: University College London's agreement covers the use of NHS England cancer registration data on infants with neuroblastoma to study long-term survival and compare England with five other European countries. The data is for understanding why survival fell in England in the 2000s and helping to identify best clinical practice. Results have been presented at conferences, including a 2026 poster concluding that observation alone appeared safe for selected infants with localised disease.

DARS-NIC-656761-R6H7W.summary: The University of Leeds's agreement covers the use of cancer registration, death registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data to run the Yorkshire Specialist Register of Cancer in Children and Young People. It supports research on hospital admissions, care pathways, late health effects and survival, aiming to improve care for young people with cancer. Reported results include published papers on long-term health problems, and evidence that supported clinical services in adopting risk-stratified follow-up care.

DARS-NIC-656762-V9J7N.summary: Queen Mary University of London's agreement covers identifiable NHS England cancer registration data on people diagnosed with invasive or in situ breast cancer, together with control groups. The data is for a case-control evaluation of the NHS Breast Screening Programme, looking at its effect on breast cancer deaths and on overdiagnosis. The agreement allows the work to inform efforts to improve the national screening programme. Two papers have been published, on the effect on breast cancer mortality and on incidence.

DARS-NIC-656763-K3F9R.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers the use of national cancer registration, hospital admission, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and cancer waiting times data to study women diagnosed with non-invasive breast cancer (ductal carcinoma in situ, DCIS). It looks at the risk of later invasive breast cancer, death from breast cancer and further non-invasive cancer. The aim is to inform screening and treatment guidance. Two published BMJ papers have already been cited in NICE and Association of Breast Surgeons guidance.

DARS-NIC-656767-M5W2L.summary: The UK Health Security Agency's agreement covers the use of cancer registration data from the National Disease Registration Service. The data is for studying cervical cancer in women under 30, comparing rates across birth cohorts by their eligibility for HPV (human papillomavirus) vaccination. The aim is to give evidence for monitoring and evaluating England's HPV vaccination programme and to inform policy. So far, the text reports that surveillance has been established, but not yet any evidence of vaccination impact.

DARS-NIC-656768-C1Z1M.summary: Imperial College London's Small Area Health Statistics Unit's agreement covers cancer registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data, some of it identifiable. The data is for research and surveillance on how cancer and other health conditions relate to environmental, social and geographical factors, aiming to inform public health policy. Reported results include a public online Environment and Health Atlas for England and Wales, launched in 2013, and 20 peer-reviewed publications in the last two years.

DARS-NIC-656770-J1L3N.summary: Royal Papworth Hospital NHS Foundation Trust's agreement covers identifiable cancer registration, hospital admission, outpatient, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for patients in its MesobanK study. The data is for adding clinical details to tissue, fluid and blood samples, so researchers can pick suitable samples for asbestos-related disease research. The aim is better understanding, diagnosis and treatment of mesothelioma. So far, MesobanK has supplied samples to over 83 research projects.

DARS-NIC-656771-F4K5X.summary: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust holds cancer registration data from the National Disease Registration Service (NDRS), originally supplied by Public Health England. The data supports a study of non-Hodgkin lymphoma in people aged 15 to 25, looking at how common it is, how it is treated and what outcomes follow. The agreement only allows the data to be kept securely. The study aims to identify the most effective treatments for each subtype and help more young people be cured.

DARS-NIC-656773-F5L2T.summary: Queen Mary University of London (QMUL) is using data on breast cancers diagnosed between routine NHS breast screening appointments, known as interval cancers. The Centre for Cancer Prevention is carrying out an independent audit for the cancer screening programmes, reporting interval cancer rates for each screening service and supporting discussions with services. The stated benefit is better information on how well the programme performs, to support quality analysis and planning.
DARS-NIC-656773-F5L2T.retense_draft: Queen Mary University of London's agreement covers data on breast cancers diagnosed between routine NHS breast screening appointments, known as interval cancers. The agreement allows the Centre for Cancer Prevention to carry out an independent audit for the cancer screening programmes, reporting interval cancer rates for each screening service and supporting discussions with services. The stated benefit is better information on how well the programme performs, to support quality analysis and planning.

DARS-NIC-656775-N0V8C.summary: The University of Bristol's agreement covers identifiable National Disease Registration Service (NDRS) cancer registration data, linked to men aged 50 to 69 in a prostate cancer screening trial. The data is for studying whether a single PSA blood test screen reduces deaths from prostate cancer and from all causes, and what screening would cost. The aim is to give evidence for UK screening policy. Results from the 10-year follow-up were published in a medical journal in 2018 and used to update patient and GP information sheets.

DARS-NIC-656777-B0V8N.summary: The University of Leeds, an academic organisation, is permitted to hold national cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data linked to survey responses from men with prostate cancer. The agreement allows the data to be used to understand factors linked to quality of life after diagnosis, and the data is kept securely while the university plans a request to re-use it. Reported results include 15 peer-reviewed articles, reports sent to every clinical team across the UK, and a Movember web tool.

DARS-NIC-656778-L3D2T.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research's agreement covers identifiable NHS England cancer registration, hospital care and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for participants in the TACT2 breast cancer trial. The agreement allows the data to be used to test whether routinely collected health data can reliably identify cancer recurrence. The intended benefit is that future breast cancer trials could use this data for long-term follow-up, reducing the burden on hospitals and participants. A poster has been presented at a Cancer Research UK conference.

DARS-NIC-656779-D9Y3Z.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research's agreement covers identifiable NHS England cancer registration, hospital (A&E, admitted patient and outpatient) and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for people who took part in the POETIC breast cancer trial. The agreement allows testing of whether routine health data can reliably show when breast cancer has returned, so that it could replace hospital-based follow-up in future trials. The intended benefit is less long-term follow-up burden for patients and hospitals.

DARS-NIC-656780-B1W0Y.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research's agreement covers identifiable NHS England cancer registration, hospital (A&E, admitted patient and outpatient) and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for participants in the IMPORT HIGH breast cancer trial. The agreement allows the data to test whether routine health data can reliably identify cancer recurrence, so that it could replace hospital-based follow-up in future trials. The main intended benefit is less burden on patients and hospital staff in long-term follow-up.

DARS-NIC-656781-W4B0L.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research's agreement covers identifiable NHS England cancer registration, hospital and systemic anti-cancer therapy records for women who took part in the FAST-Forward breast radiotherapy trial. The agreement allows testing of whether routinely collected health data can reliably identify breast cancer recurrence, so long-term trial follow-up need not depend on hospital-collected data. The intended benefit is less follow-up burden on hospitals and future trial participants.

DARS-NIC-656784-C7P5B.summary: The Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP)'s agreement covers linked cancer registration, treatment, hospital and patient experience data for the National Audit of Breast Cancer in Older Patients. The audit looks at the care and outcomes of women over 70 with breast cancer in England and Wales, compared with women aged 50 to 70. It aims to give NHS providers comparative information to improve care. So far it has delivered national audit reports and quality improvement tools, and 12 published papers.

DARS-NIC-656793-T4H6S.summary: The University of Bristol's agreement covers NHS England cancer, hospital inpatient and outpatient, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and diagnostic imaging data for the ProtecT trial. The trial compares surgery, radiotherapy and active monitoring for men with low- or intermediate-risk localised prostate cancer, and the data are for following their outcomes over about 20 years. The data are for giving patients and clinicians evidence for treatment decisions. Results from earlier follow-ups were published in the New England Journal of Medicine and have affected treatment guidelines.

DARS-NIC-656794-C7Q5X.summary: The Institute of Cancer Research's agreement covers identifiable cancer registration data on men aged 18 to 79 diagnosed with breast cancer in England and Wales. The agreement allows the data to be used to invite men into a case-control study of the genetic, environmental and behavioural causes of male breast cancer. The aim is better evidence on risk for patients, families and doctors. The study has reported findings, including links with obesity, infertility and genetic risk, which help doctors identify high-risk men.

DARS-NIC-656800-V6B5C.summary: Cancer Research UK's agreement covers the use of national cancer registration, hospital admission, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data about people with non-small cell lung cancer. The data is for evaluating which patient, tumour and provider factors affect access to treatment, and whether access varies between NHS trusts, including chemoradiotherapy and targeted therapies. The main intended benefit is to help those delivering lung cancer services reduce unwarranted variation and improve equitable access to treatment.

DARS-NIC-656801-R9F6Z.summary: University College London (UCL) is using record-level hospital, emergency care and cancer registry data linked to about 10,500 participants in the STAMPEDE prostate cancer trial. It is comparing this data with the information the trial collects itself, covering survival, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, second-line treatment and toxicities. The aim is to show whether routine healthcare data could make trials more efficient. Reported results include a published finding that radiotherapy reduced the risk of urinary tract obstruction, and a published finding that zoledronic acid reduced the risk of fractures.
DARS-NIC-656801-R9F6Z.retense_draft: University College London's agreement covers the linking of record-level hospital, emergency care and cancer registry data with the data of about 10,500 participants in the STAMPEDE prostate cancer trial. The data is for comparing it with the information the trial collects itself, covering survival, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, second-line treatment and toxicities. The aim is to show whether routine healthcare data could make trials more efficient. Reported results include a published finding that radiotherapy reduced the risk of urinary tract obstruction, and a published finding that zoledronic acid reduced the risk of fractures.

DARS-NIC-656805-R5Z2Y.summary: Cancer Research UK's agreement covers pseudonymised National Disease Registration Service data on women diagnosed with ovarian cancer in 2015 and 2016, linked to hospital admissions and systemic anti-cancer therapy records. The agreement allows the data to be used to study how access to ovarian cancer treatment varies across England, and how far patient characteristics and healthcare system factors explain this. The aim is to give evidence that could help reduce variation in care.

DARS-NIC-656806-N9V7N.summary: University College London's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised NHS cancer registration, hospital, diagnostic imaging, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for people in the Add-Aspirin cancer trial. The agreement allows this routine data to be compared with the trial's own follow-up to see whether it can reliably record outcomes such as survival and cancer recurrence. The aim is to make cancer trials more efficient and less costly. A 2021 paper already described how to access such data for trials.

DARS-NIC-656811-F7T9C.summary: Clatterbridge Cancer Centre NHS Foundation Trust's agreement covers national cancer registration, treatment, and hospital records for people with blood cancer. The agreement allows the data to be used to study how COVID-19 infection affected them and how the pandemic changed their diagnosis, treatment and outcomes. The main intended benefit is to identify who is most at risk, so patients can be protected and treated more appropriately. The project has secured over £400,000 of research funding and involved patient groups, though no analysis has yet been done.

DARS-NIC-656813-F4H5W.summary: University College London (UCL), working with GRAIL, LLC, is permitted under its agreement to use record-level cancer registration, hospital, emergency care, radiotherapy, systemic anti-cancer therapy and related data on people in the SUMMIT study. The agreement allows the data to be used to see which cancers participants develop and to assess low-dose CT lung cancer screening and the GRAIL multi-cancer blood test. The main intended benefit is stronger evidence for a national lung cancer screening programme and earlier cancer detection.

DARS-NIC-656815-R5X0N.summary: The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine's agreement covers linked NHS cancer data, including registrations, waiting times, hospital records, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy. The data is for studying where patients choose to have specialist cancer treatment and how centralising services affects travel, fairness of access and outcomes. The aim is to give evidence to guide how cancer services are designed. Reported benefits include centralisation models being adopted by NHS England and analysis supporting management of the cancer backlog.

DARS-NIC-656816-Z3N6R.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers linked National Disease Registration Service data on cancer registrations, hospital care, imaging, radiotherapy and chemotherapy for women with invasive breast cancer. The agreement allows checking how accurately an algorithm using routine data identifies breast cancer recurrence, compared with the AZURE trial's recurrence records. The aim is reliable recurrence information to support treatment comparisons and patient prognosis. A peer-reviewed paper on the algorithm was published in BJC Reports in 2025.

DARS-NIC-656818-N1B5Q.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers NHS England cancer registration, treatment, hospital and radiotherapy data on women diagnosed with early breast cancer. The agreement allows the data to be used to describe survival, second cancers and other diseases, and to build predictions of the benefits and risks of treatment options. The main intended benefit is that patients and clinicians can make better-informed treatment decisions. Earlier work has already been cited in major breast cancer guidelines, including those from NICE, and used in clinician training.

DARS-NIC-656823-G0Q2C.summary: The University of Leeds's agreement covers the use of cancer registration, hospital admissions and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for patients in England who have cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a liver cancer. The data is for studying how patients' characteristics and where they live affect which treatment they receive, how long they survive and how their liver disease progresses. The agreement allows the team to hope this will reveal variations in clinical practice and help improve future resource allocation and outcomes.

DARS-NIC-656824-R8K0V.summary: Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, working with The Christie NHS Foundation Trust, is using identifiable cancer registration, hospital admission, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for lung cancer patients treated with curative-intent radiotherapy. They are studying how radiotherapy dose to the heart relates to survival and cardiac death, so that sensitive areas can be given dose limits and side effects reduced. A benefit already reported is that the work informed a dose limit to the base of the heart at The Christie, now being monitored by the RAPID-RT study, and results were presented at ESTRO conferences.
DARS-NIC-656824-R8K0V.retense_draft: Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, working with The Christie NHS Foundation Trust, is allowed to use identifiable cancer registration, hospital admission, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for lung cancer patients treated with curative-intent radiotherapy. The agreement covers studying how radiotherapy dose to the heart relates to survival and cardiac death, so that sensitive areas can be given dose limits and side effects reduced. A benefit already reported is that the work informed a dose limit to the base of the heart at The Christie, now being monitored by the RAPID-RT study, and results were presented at ESTRO conferences.

DARS-NIC-656825-X7T4K.summary: University College London (UCL)'s agreement covers NDRS cancer registration data, covering cancer diagnoses and mortality, for the Advancing Survivorship after Cancer: Outcomes Trial. The trial tests a booklet and health professional feedback aimed at helping cancer survivors improve their health behaviours. The data is for assessing whether the intervention improves cancer outcomes and survival, so it could become part of standard NHS care. Earlier data was used to classify participants by diagnosis for analyses in papers due for submission.

DARS-NIC-656826-M3Y6C.summary: Cancer Research UK's agreement covers pseudonymised, aggregated NDRS Cancer Registrations data on cancer incidence in England, covering 1999 to 2022. The agreement allows it to produce statistics and trends on cancer incidence by factors such as sex, age and stage of diagnosis, answer public queries, and estimate cancers linked to risk factors. These are published on its website and in public reports. The main intended benefit is up-to-date evidence on the state of cancer in the UK for policy-makers, clinicians and patients.

DARS-NIC-656827-P2X2W.summary: The University of Liverpool's agreement covers the use of national cancer registration and lung cancer audit data for the UK Lung cancer Screening (UKLS) trial. The data is for checking long-term outcomes for participants and non-participants, and for testing whether predicted lung cancer risk matches actual cases. The findings are expected to support evidence-based decisions on care. The university has already published papers in Thorax and The Lancet Regional Health - Europe, including an updated risk model and trial results on lung cancer mortality.

DARS-NIC-656830-C3F5S.summary: The University of Leeds's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised cancer registration and systemic anti-cancer therapy (chemotherapy) data on people diagnosed with cancer aged 12 to 29. The research looks at whether the dose and intensity of chemotherapy affect one-year and three-year survival, and what makes it harder for patients to receive the ideal dose. The aim is to guide changes in how these patients are treated and to improve outcomes.

DARS-NIC-656832-M8F7G.summary: The University of Nottingham's agreement covers national cancer registration data from the National Disease Registration Service (NDRS). The data is for finding out how much healthy tissue should be removed around a breast tumour known as ductal carcinoma in-situ (DCIS) during breast conserving surgery. The agreement allows comparison of the measured margin width with outcomes such as cancer recurrence and survival, with the aim of establishing the optimum margin width.

DARS-NIC-656834-N7Z3Q.summary: Barts Health NHS Trust's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised hospital, cancer registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy records for people treated for retinoblastoma, a childhood eye cancer, or who carry an RB1 gene mutation. The study looks at whether the type of gene mutation, and the treatment given, affects the risk of developing a second tumour elsewhere in the body later in life. The main intended benefit is closer monitoring of higher-risk patients, which could lead to earlier diagnosis and treatment.

DARS-NIC-656836-T2J0T.summary: Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust holds pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, cancer waiting times and radiotherapy records from a completed breast cancer clinical trial (the BEA trial). It keeps them securely so the trial analysis can be reconstructed or checked if challenged. The original analysis looked at how socioeconomic status, obesity and diabetes relate to breast cancer recurrence and death, aiming to improve survival and reduce unwarranted variations in care. A draft journal article has been submitted but is not yet published.

DARS-NIC-656837-J7G8S.summary: Erasmus University Medical Centre's agreement covers identifiable NHS England cancer registration data on people in England diagnosed with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (a skin cancer) in 2013 to 2015. The data is for building and validating a model that predicts the risk of the cancer spreading, and for comparing it with current staging systems. The aim is to help clinicians decide on follow-up care. A prediction model has already been developed, published and made available as an online app, and it performed better than current staging systems.

DARS-NIC-656838-J7H7S.summary: Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and patient experience data on adults in England with brain tumours. The data is for describing patterns of care, outcomes and costs, and for assessing how care varies and how this relates to outcomes and costs. It also allows comparing the effect of tumour biology with that of treatment. The study team has published several abstracts and articles on topics including glioblastoma costs and end-of-life care.

DARS-NIC-656839-K5V9L.summary: Queen Mary University of London's agreement covers pseudonymised cancer registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data, linked to GP and hospital records in the QResearch database. The agreement allows the data to support medical research into causes of disease, treatments and outcomes, including COVID-19 risk prediction, and allows approved UK universities to use the data. The aim is research that benefits patients and the NHS. Reported benefits include the QCancer and QCOVID risk tools, used in clinical practice.

DARS-NIC-656841-D0P8Y.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers the use of pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and waiting-time data on people diagnosed with primary central nervous system (CNS) tumours. The data is for studying how common these tumours are, survival, treatments and later health events, with the aim of informing guidelines and care. A paper on incidence trends has been published in Neuro-Oncology, and the work led to the Brain Tumour Data Improvement Initiative.

DARS-NIC-656842-S5V7V.summary: NHS England, with the Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP) and the Royal College of Surgeons' Clinical Effectiveness Unit, is covered by an agreement allowing use of national cancer registration, treatment, hospital and patient survey data. The agreement allows this data to run the audits of bowel cancer and oesophago-gastric cancer care in England and Wales. The aim is to help services compare themselves, share good practice and improve patient care. Reported results include annual reports with recommendations, and improvements such as more patients with oesophageal high-grade dysplasia being discussed by specialist teams.

DARS-NIC-656843-D8M4Z.summary: University Hospitals Plymouth NHS Trust's agreement covers pseudonymised national cancer registration, hospital outpatient, treatment, audit and patient-survey data on people diagnosed with colorectal cancer in England between 2000 and 2014. The agreement allows the study of the demographics and long-term survival of young patients (aged 40 and under) and comparison with older patients. The results may help inform screening, public awareness and management of young colorectal cancer patients. Early analysis found regional differences in patient age, deprivation, diagnosis and five-year survival, with findings due for publication.

DARS-NIC-656845-G9J9W.summary: Southampton City Council's Public Health team's agreement covers pseudonymised NDRS Cancer Registrations data on cancers diagnosed in Southampton residents and in patients registered with Southampton GP practices. The data is for auditing cancer health inequalities, including by area deprivation and Primary Care Network, to inform local needs assessments, service planning and targeted prevention. The aim is earlier diagnosis. Earlier analysis was used in GP packs and by NHS colleagues in local planning, and the latest data produced a public cancer web page and dashboard.

DARS-NIC-656847-K4L8H.summary: The University of Newcastle upon Tyne's agreement covers linked national cancer registration, hospital, treatment, lung cancer audit and molecular test data. It allows study of whether access to targeted therapies and immunotherapies differs by factors such as deprivation, and how survival varies. The data is for informing policy and services so that treatment access is fairer. A published 2023 paper found that non-small cell lung cancer patients in the most deprived areas were 55% less likely to receive these treatments.

DARS-NIC-656848-T9J1Q.summary: The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) runs the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD), which links GP records to National Disease Registration Service cancer registration data. Approved researchers use the linked, pseudonymised data for observational health research, aiming to improve clinical care, public health policy and regulatory decisions. Published studies have already shown higher flu risks in cancer survivors, which supported vaccination priority guidance.

DARS-NIC-656849-P9M6C.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers pseudonymised cancer registry, hospital, imaging, radiotherapy and chemotherapy records for people in England diagnosed with lymphoma between 1997 and 2020. The data is for studying how radiotherapy use varies, how to predict lymphoma recurrence, and long-term effects such as heart disease and second cancers. The aim is to improve understanding of the best management of lymphoma subtypes. Research from this study has already been cited in clinical guidelines and has helped shape clinical trials.

DARS-NIC-656850-Y1V4Q.summary: Leiden University's agreement covers national cancer registration data, linked hospital records, radiotherapy data and systemic anti-cancer therapy data. The data is for comparing treatment and survival for patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) across European countries in the EURECCA consortium. The stated aim is to improve understanding of the epidemiology and treatment of GIST in Europe.

DARS-NIC-656851-D6M5H.summary: The Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP), with NHS England, is permitted to use pseudonymised cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy and chemotherapy data on men in England diagnosed with prostate cancer. The Royal College of Surgeons of England runs the National Prostate Cancer Audit, which assesses care and outcomes and compares NHS providers. The aim is to show where care is good and where it can improve. So far, the audit reports fewer under-treated and over-treated patients, and has held two quality improvement workshops.

DARS-NIC-656854-T9G6P.summary: The University of Manchester's agreement covers national cancer registration, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data. The agreement allows the university to estimate how many patients were cured by radical treatment, meaning no death or further treatment within five years. The data is for assessing how much each treatment type contributes, and for examining differences by cancer site, deprivation, ethnic group and age. The expected benefit is scientific publications and conference abstracts. Abstracts have already been presented at scientific conferences.

DARS-NIC-656855-D5T2Z.summary: The University of Oxford's agreement covers national cancer data, including records of cancer registrations, hospital care, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy (SACT). The data is for studying survival and serious side effects in patients given cancer drugs in routine NHS care, and what influences these outcomes. The aim is to give patients and clinicians a better picture of real-world outcomes than clinical trials alone. The work so far has produced evidence on treatment patterns and outcomes, including in older patients.

DARS-NIC-656857-F4D9R.summary: The University of Cambridge's agreement covers identifiable cancer registration, outpatient, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data for people diagnosed with breast, endometrial or ovarian cancer. The SEARCH study looks at how inherited genetic variation affects cancer risk, tumour subtypes, treatment response and survival. Results are intended for peer-reviewed publications. The study's results have already contributed to CanRisk, a cancer risk prediction tool, and PREDICT breast, a prognosis tool used by healthcare professionals.

DARS-NIC-656858-Y9D0P.summary: The University of Leeds's agreement covers linking cancer registration, hospital admission, outpatient, radiotherapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy data to questionnaire responses from consenting bladder cancer patients in Yorkshire, Humber, South Tees and North Derbyshire. The data is for describing patients' health-related quality of life, understanding variation in outcomes and identifying unmet needs, to help improve services. Published papers so far include studies on quality of life after treatment and on sexual function after diagnosis.

DARS-NIC-656860-Q5Q9Q.summary: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, with King's College London, is using identifiable cancer registration, hospital, radiotherapy and chemotherapy data on women with lobular or ductal in situ breast cancer who joined the GLACIER and ICICLE studies. They are following up survival and disease progression to see whether genes and tumour markers affect outcomes. The aim is to predict who is likely to develop invasive disease, so treatment can be targeted. The original studies found new links between genetic variations and further breast disease.
